Created at the Brown Hotel in Louisville in 1926, to feed late-night dancers.
Peanut butter and marshmallow creme. In 2006 one Massachusetts lawmaker tried to curb it in schools; another proposed it as the state sandwich.
Named after Dagwood Bumstead, the comic-strip husband who builds towering ones at midnight.
Peanut butter and banana, sometimes with bacon, fried: said to be Elvis Presley's favourite.
Sometimes called the Chinese hamburger, and often said to be one of the oldest sandwiches in the world.
Cape Town's giant roll of chips and meat, said to be named after a 1976 screening of The Great Gatsby.
Durban's curry in a hollowed-out loaf, served with the scooped-out bread on top.
Uruguay's national sandwich. Legend says a customer asked for kid goat, chivito, and was given beef instead.
A New York bodega classic: minced beef and cheese chopped on the griddle and piled into a roll.
Mrs Beeton's recipe to tempt an invalid: thin cold toast between two slices of bread and butter. The Royal Society of Chemistry revived it in 2011.
Guadalajara's 'drowned sandwich', soaked in spicy tomato sauce.
A tamale stuffed inside a bread roll: breakfast in Mexico City.
Named after the Chilean president Ramón Barros Luco, who always ordered beef with melted cheese.
Turkey, cream cheese and strawberry jam, named after the Havana socialite who ordered it.
Chicago's Puerto Rican sandwich, with flattened fried plantain in place of bread.
Florence's tripe sandwich, sold from street carts, with the bread dipped in the broth.
Sweden's 'sandwich cake': layers of bread and fillings, iced with mayonnaise and decorated like a gateau.
Dutch for 'bouncer': fried eggs on bread, said to be the last dish served before closing time.
French for 'submachine gun': Belgium's half baguette loaded with meat, sauce and chips.
Cologne's 'half a rooster' is a rye roll with a thick slice of Dutch cheese, mustard and onion. There is no bird in it.
